analysis.one_liner: Requires large meatpackers to buy a quarter of their livestock through open bidding instead of their own supply arrangements.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Agriculture Committee: it was referred there on August 1, 2002 and died when the 107th Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force large meatpacking companies to buy at least 25% of the cattle they slaughter on the open 'spot' market, where ranchers can shop their animals to multiple buyers and bidding sets the price (cooperatives owned by farmers would have a lower 12.5% requirement). Packers that reported heavy 'captive supply' — cattle they already own or control through contracts — would phase into that requirement between 2004 and 2008. The goal is to give independent ranchers real price competition instead of selling into a market where a few big companies control most of their own supply. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent livestock producers, especially cattle ranchers who currently sell into a market where a handful of multi-plant packers buy most cattle through contracts with a few large feedlots or their own animals. A guaranteed open-market share would force packers to bid publicly for a slice of every day's slaughter, improving price discovery and giving small producers competitive bids they often cannot get today. States could also require higher percentages since the bill does not preempt stronger state rules.

how_it_helps.text: Covered packers must slaughter at least 25% of each plant's daily volume through spot market sales from nonaffiliated producers, with 12.5% for producer cooperatives, guaranteeing a floor of open, competitive bidding.

A 'spot market sale' requires a firm base price and a 'reasonable competitive bidding opportunity,' meaning no contract or practice may block the producer from soliciting bids from other packers — so the mandated purchases create genuine price discovery rather than nominal sales.

'Nonaffiliated producer' is defined so the required open-market purchases cannot be filled with animals in which the packer has an equity stake or that are controlled by the packer's own officers or owners, closing the easiest loophole.
Packers reporting more than 75% captive supply in 2001 face a staged phase-in — 5% in 2004–05, 15% in 2006–07, and 25% from 2008 — so the largest captive-supply operators cannot avoid the rule.
The bill does not preempt state rules requiring a higher spot-market percentage, allowing states to go further.

analysis.who_pays: Large multi-plant meatpacking companies that rely on captive supply — long-term contracts, formula deals, and their own cattle — would lose flexibility and would have to bid on the open market for a quarter of their slaughter volume. Packers that own only one plant are exempt, and producer cooperatives get a lower requirement. Some of the added procurement cost could eventually show up in wholesale meat prices, though competitive bidding is also meant to reduce packers' market power.

drawbacks.text: A packer that owns only one processing plant is excluded from the definition of a covered packer, so single-plant operations — including large ones — face no open-market requirement at all.

Producer cooperatives are held to only half the spot-market requirement of other packers (12.5% versus 25%), a carve-out that preserves more captive-supply arrangements for cooperative packers than for their corporate competitors.

Forcing a quarter of every plant's daily slaughter onto the spot market is a blunt instrument: it constrains packers and the large feedlots that have invested in contracting relationships, and it could raise procurement costs that are partly passed to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: ranchers would get genuine bidding and better price information, while the biggest packers would lose the captive-supply arrangements that give them predictable, cheap cattle. The bill is imperfectly designed — the single-plant exemption and the cooperative carve-out both narrow its reach — but its main provisions are straightforward and phased in over several years, which softens the transition cost. The objections that matter most are about cost pass-through and about whether mandated spot percentages address competition better than other remedies; they are serious but not enough to outweigh the transparency benefit for producers who today sell into a thin market.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley introduced the bill on August 1, 2002, for himself and Senator Russ Feingold, as a measure to increase competition and transparency among livestock packers.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
That was the bill's last action: the committee never reported it out, no hearing or vote is recorded, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies that depend on captive-supply cattle arrangements are better off, because the open-bidding mandate never got a hearing, let alone a vote, before the Congress expired.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Tom Harkin (D-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 1, 2002 and never held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it to the Senate.

against.name: Large meatpacking companies and their trade groups
against.role: Multi-plant packers reliant on captive-supply cattle
against.what_they_did: Opposed livestock competition reforms, including captive-supply limits, during the 2002 farm bill debate.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican from Iowa sponsored the bill with a Wisconsin Democrat as its one cosponsor, and there is no recorded party-split vote because the bill never reached the floor.

industries.note: They would have to buy at least 25% of each plant's daily slaughter through open, competitive bidding from nonaffiliated producers, with the heaviest captive-supply operators phased in from 2004 to 2008. Their interest in keeping formula contracts and packer-owned cattle runs directly against ranchers' access to competitive bids.

Cooperative packers are covered by the rule but at half the spot-market requirement (12.5% instead of 25%), and with a higher captive-supply trigger (87.5%). Because these co-ops are producer-owned, their members sit on both sides of the trade-off between contract flexibility and open-market price discovery.

The bill's required spot-market share cannot be filled with animals in which the packer holds equity or that are affiliated with packer officers and owners, so cattle the packers control themselves would displace no mandated purchases — shrinking the volume those operations sell to packers.
A guaranteed open-bidding share forces packers to bid publicly for part of every day's slaughter, improving the prices and price information available to producers selling on the spot market.
